name: Reaction time
seoDesc: Reaction time: work out reaction time (First attempt) from the distance. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Reaction time calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports reaction time (First attempt) immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Reaction time calculator work?
sections.html:
The Reaction time calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports reaction time (First attempt) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the distance (First attempt), the distance (Second attempt), the distance (Third attempt) and the distance (Fourth attempt).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Reaction time calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Reaction time=the square root of (2) × the square root of (distance ÷ G)
Average reaction time=((1 ÷ 2) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 2) × reaction time)
Average reaction time=((1 ÷ 3) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 3) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 3) × reaction time)
Average reaction time=((1 ÷ 4) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 4) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 4) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 4) × reaction time)
Distance=(1 ÷ 2) × G × (reaction time ^ 2)
Average reaction time=((1 ÷ 5) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 5) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 5) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 5) × reaction time + (1 ÷ 5) × reaction time)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Time, opening in milliseconds

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Reaction time calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Reaction time calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns reaction time (First attempt), derived from the distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Reaction time calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance (First attempt) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance (First attempt) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Reaction time calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
